# Three ways to index a vector

An index makes nearest-neighbour search fast by looking at a small part of the table instead of all
of it. Postgres can now index a `vector` column in three ways: pgvector's **HNSW**, Timescale's
**DiskANN** from pgvectorscale, and **PRISM** from the newer pg_vectorsearch. The first two are
graphs that a query walks, and the third is a set of partitions that a query scans.

The lab built all three on the same table and measured build time, size, latency and recall. Recall
is the share of the true nearest neighbours that the index returns; recall@10 asks how many of the
exact top 10 it finds.

## The contenders

**HNSW** (pgvector) is a layered proximity graph. A query enters at the sparse top layer and
descends towards the dense bottom one, keeping `ef_search` candidates as it goes. It needs no
training pass and inserts are cheap. Two settings trade build time for recall: `m`, the links per
node, and `ef_construction`.

**DiskANN** (pgvectorscale 0.9.1) is a single flat graph, built to stay fast when it does not fit in
memory. It keeps compressed vectors in the index (statistical binary quantization). A rescore step
then re-reads the full vectors for the best candidates.

**PRISM** (pg_vectorsearch 0.1.0, alpha, Postgres 18 only) is not a graph. k-means splits the table
into `nlist` partitions, in the style of an IVF index, and each vector is stored as a RaBitQ code
with an error bound. A query scans the `prism.nprobe` nearest partitions. It re-reads full vectors
only for the candidates that the error bound cannot settle. PRISM indexes pgvector's column in
place:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON demo_docs USING prism (embedding vec32_cosine_ops);  -- build after loading
SET prism.nprobe = 40;                                               -- 0 = auto
SELECT * FROM prism_index_settings('demo_docs_embedding_idx');       -- what it chose, and why
```

## The measurement

The test used 20,000 random 64-dimensional unit vectors on Postgres 18, in one run on a laptop, with
recall@10 measured against an exact scan:

| index | build | size | best recall@10 | ms per query at best |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HNSW (m 16, ef_construction 64) | 2.7 s | 11.4 MB | 0.99 (ef_search 400) | 3.3 |
| DiskANN (defaults) | 20.3 s | 9.1 MB | 0.76 (search list 400, rescore 400) | 8.3 |
| PRISM (auto nlist 144) | 0.3 s | 1.8 MB | 0.98 (nprobe 160, every list) | 3.0 |

Here PRISM builds about nine times faster than HNSW and takes a sixth of its size. Its recall nearly
matches HNSW's once every partition is probed. The automatic `nprobe` (10 here) reaches only about
0.40, and recall rises to 0.81 at 40 and 0.93 at 80.

::: {.callout-important}
## Read the test data, not just the table

Random vectors are the worst case for both quantization and partitioning. Their coordinates are
independent, so binary codes have nothing to capture and k-means has no clusters to follow. That is
why DiskANN stalls at 0.76 and PRISM needs every partition. Real embeddings cluster strongly, and on
them both indexes do far better; PRISM's automatic `nprobe` aims at a recall of about 0.95. Treat
the table as a comparison under stress, not a verdict.
:::

## Choosing

- **HNSW** is the default. It needs no training, it is mature, and it gives good recall at any size
  that fits in memory.
- **DiskANN** suits an index that will not fit in RAM, when you can afford the slower build.
- **PRISM** suits cases where build time and size matter, such as frequent rebuilds or many tables.
  It needs Postgres 18, and as an alpha it may need `DROP EXTENSION` and a rebuild between releases.

In SQLAlchemy all three are an `Index(...)` with `postgresql_using` and `postgresql_ops`, and the
queries do not change.
